newsitem.title: USA: GPU looking at all areas of operation.
newsitem.headline: GPU looking at all areas of operation.

text.p: GPU Inc's decision to study the sale or early retirement of its Oyster Creek Nuclear Generating Station is part of a look at the economics of the entire company, President Fred D. Hafer said Thursday.
The company is "looking at all areas of our operation," he told a teleconference with reporters.
The facility is one of the oldest and most expensive nuclear power plants in the U.S., reporters were told.
Oyster Creek is the oldest operating nuclear power plant in the U.S., according to the Nuclear Energy Institute.
Hafer said the plant, built by General Electric Co at a cost of $90 million, went into commercial operation in December 1969.
Because of upgrades made since, the plant's current on the company's books is $700 million.
The plant's age, by itself, is not one of the factors resulting in the decision to look at sale or early retirement, GPU Nuclear Inc chief executive T. Gary Broughton said.
He said its marginal costs for operation, maintenance and fuel are in the fourth quartile for U.S. nuclear plants.
This puts its variable cost of operation -- the amount that can not be avoided by shutting the plant down -- at around $0.037 per kilowatt hour, GPU Energy President Dennis Baldassari said.
That compares with today's market price for wholesale power purchases of $0.02 to $0.025 per kilowatt hour.
Broughton said this is because Oyster Creek is one of the smallest nuclear plants in operation, which means the overhead is spread over fewer kilowatts.

The overhead costs are exacerbated by the fact GPU has only two nuclear plants, Hafer said, pointing out that a buyer with current nuclear operations could spread costs over a larger number of kilowatt hours.
GPU said earlier on Thursday that it does not plan to close its other nuclear plant, Three Mile Island Unit 1, an 819 megawatt unit that went into operation in 1974.
Broughton said GPU has 900 employees devoted to Oyster Creek at the plant site in Lacey Township, N.J. and company headquarters in Parsippany, N.J.
Oyster Creek will run through the fall of 2000 "if we decide to retire" the plant, he said, noting that is when the plant's spent fuel storage capacity is expected to be used up.

Broughton said the company has no estimate on the manpower that will be needed for decommissioning. This will take a minimum of five years, he said, adding it is "more realistic" to expect it to take seven to eight years.
Once the decommissioning is completed the farm land that forms a buffer around the plant will be available for other uses.
